accrington.hook: The "Owd Reds" of a cotton town, playing on a cricket field: the smallest of the founders, and the first to leave.
history: Accrington Football Club was formed in 1878 at a meeting in a town pub and made its home on the cricket club's field at Thorneyholme Road, where the footballers took the western end. They played in red, which gave them the name the Owd Reds.

The club was ambitious early: it was thrown out of the Football Association in 1883 for paying a player, a year before the wider row over professionalism came to a head. By 1888 it was strong enough to be chosen among the twelve founders of the Football League, the smallest town of the twelve.

Accrington held their own in the first seasons, with England half-back George Haworth at their heart and a teenage forward, Johnny Kirkham, who would become the club's record appearance maker and scorer. Their best finish, sixth, came in 1889-90.

seasons.1888-89: Accrington opened with a 1-2 defeat at Everton, then drew 5-5 at Blackburn Rovers, where 19-year-old Kirkham scored twice on debut. Bob Brand's hat-trick, the club's first in the League, beat Derby County 6-2 on 13 October, and on 20 October goalkeeper Johnny Horne's defence held Preston North End's "Invincibles" to their only scoreless game of the season. Draws were the theme (eight of them) and Accrington finished seventh on 20 points, level with Everton. Billy Barbour (13) and Kirkham (12) led the scoring; Horne and full-back John Stevenson played every league and cup game. In the Cup, Blackburn were held 1-1 at Thorneyholme Road but won the replay 5-0.

aston-villa.hook: The Cup holders of 1887 and home of William McGregor, the man who invented the League; a fast, short-passing Birmingham side.
history: Villa were founded in 1874 by young men from a Wesleyan chapel cricket team in Aston, who wanted a winter game. In 1876 they took on a rented field at Perry Barr. That same year a Glaswegian, George Ramsay, happened on one of their practice games in Aston Park and was asked to join in. He became captain and taught the team the Scottish passing game.

Villa won the Birmingham Senior Cup in 1880, and with Archie Hunter as captain they won the FA Cup in 1887, beating West Bromwich Albion 2-0 at the Oval. They were the first Midlands club to win it. In March 1888 Villa committee man William McGregor wrote to the leading clubs proposing a league with fixed fixtures. The Football League was the result, and Villa were among its twelve founders.

seasons.1888-89: Villa's first League game was a 1-1 draw at Wolves on 8 September. Tommy Green scored, and Gershom Cox put through his own goal. They beat Stoke 5-1 in the first League match at Wellington Road, then thrashed Notts County 9-1, with Albert Allen scoring the club's first League hat-trick. On 1 October Archie Goodall arrived from Preston, the first in-season transfer the League approved. He scored 7 goals in 14 games. Villa won every home game until Preston won 2-0 at Perry Barr on 9 February, and finished second, a long way behind the Invincibles. Allen was top scorer with 19 in all competitions. The season ended badly: an 8-1 FA Cup thrashing at Blackburn and a 5-2 defeat at Derby.

birmingham-st-georges.hook: The brewery-backed "Dragons" of Cape Hill, rated one of the Midlands' best four yet left out of the League.
history: St George's began in Aston in 1875 and moved west to Smethwick when Harry Mitchell, son of the Cape Hill brewery owner, gave them a home and jobs for players. By 1888 the press counted them among the four best teams in the Midlands, but the League wanted one club per town and Aston Villa had Birmingham. Dropping "Mitchell" from the name, they joined the Combination and reached the last eight of the Cup before losing at Preston.

blackburn-rovers.hook: Three FA Cups in a row (1884-86): the old cup kings of the cotton town, now chasing League glory with a mix of veterans and young goalscorers.
history: Rovers were founded in 1875 by two young men just back from Shrewsbury School, and they wore the blue and white halves that are still the club's colours. They had no fixed home at first. In 1881 they built a proper ground at Leamington Road, with a grandstand for about 700 people.

Blackburn was a football-mad mill town. Rovers were the first provincial club to reach an FA Cup Final, in 1882, and then won the Cup three years running, 1884 to 1886. Their Scots included Fergus Suter, a Glasgow stonemason who came over from Darwen in 1880 and is often called the first professional footballer.
In 1888 Rovers were founder members of the Football League. They were unbeaten at Leamington Road in its first season and finished fourth.

seasons.1888-89: Rovers' first League game was a 5-5 home draw with Accrington. The season stayed high-scoring: 7-1 at Burnley with a Jack Southworth hat-trick, and 4-4 with Bolton. The low point was a 6-1 defeat at Villa in October. Southworth, a violinist off the field, was top scorer with 21 goals. Herby Arthur and Jimmy Forrest gave the side experience, and the club's first Scottish professional, Fergus Suter, made one last League appearance on 22 December. In the Cup, Rovers took revenge on Villa in round three, winning 8-1 in front of 12,000 at Leamington Road: Southworth scored four and Haresnape three. Wolves stopped them in the semi-final after a replay at Crewe.

bolton-wanderers.hook: The church-school side whose Kenny Davenport is credited with the first goal ever scored in the Football League.
history: Bolton Wanderers began in 1874 as the football team of Christ Church in Bolton, started by the curate and the master of the church school. After falling out with the vicar the players left the church grounds in 1877 and, having moved between three pitches in four years, took the name Wanderers.

From 1880-81 they settled at Pike's Lane, a rough ground with banked sides that players and spectators alike grumbled about. Under secretary J. J. Bentley, a sharp-penned football journalist and one of the men who helped William McGregor build the Football League, Bolton became one of its twelve founder members in 1888.

On the League's opening day, 8 September 1888, Bolton's local inside-right Kenny Davenport scored after a couple of minutes against Derby County, the goal now credited as the first in Football League history. Bolton still lost 6-3, but a free-scoring side led by James Brogan, Davenport and David Weir finished a respectable fifth.

seasons.1888-89: Bolton lost their first three games, the opener 3-6 at home to Derby despite Davenport's two goals, then beat Everton 6-2 with braces from Davenport, Harry Tyrer and John Milne. The autumn was patchy (a 5-1 win at West Bromwich two days after losing at Everton), but the winter brought a strong run: Weir's hat-trick beat Accrington 4-1 just before Christmas, and in March Bolton won 4-0 at Notts County and 7-3 in the return, Davenport scoring three. Five men (Brogan, Davenport, Milne, Weir, Bob Roberts) played all 22 league games. Brogan was top scorer with 13 league goals, ahead of Davenport (11) and Weir (10). The reserves went out of the FA Cup in Belfast, 0-4 to Linfield Athletic.

bootle.hook: Merseyside's other club, passed over for Everton, with the first black international, Andrew Watson.
history: Bootle began as a church team in 1879 and became Everton's main local rival. When the Football League formed, William McGregor invited Everton to represent Liverpool, so Bootle went into the Combination. Their great signing was Andrew Watson, three times capped by Scotland and widely seen as the first black international footballer, who joined in 1887. In the Cup they drew the unbeaten champions Preston.

burnley.hook: A former rugby club from a cotton town that hired Scots by the trainload and got a royal visit before it got a league.
history: Burnley began life as Burnley Rovers, a rugby club. In May 1882 its members voted to take up the association game, dropped the "Rovers" and, early in 1883, accepted the cricket club's invitation to play at Turf Moor, where the club has stayed ever since.

Burnley moved fast and broke rules doing it. The committee paid players, signed a stream of Scots and named Dan Friel captain. When the Football Association still banned professionals, Burnley led the breakaway British Football Association in 1884, and the FA gave way and legalised pay in 1885.

In 1886 Prince Albert Victor watched Burnley play Bolton at Turf Moor, the first royal to visit a football ground, and the club marked it by wearing the Prince of Wales's arms on its shirts. Two years later Burnley were one of the twelve founders of the Football League.

seasons.1888-89: Burnley lost 5-2 at Preston on opening day, Gallocher scoring their first League goal, then won 4-3 at Bolton the next week with William Tait scoring the League's first hat-trick. Tait was gone by late October after a drinking episode and a missed match. The defence leaked goals: 6-1 at Notts County (where Bob Jardine scored five) and a 7-1 home thrashing by Blackburn, a game in which forward Fred Poland is said to have kept goal (single source). Walter Cox arrived in goal in November, William McKay came from Hearts and finished as top League scorer, and a winter run including a 4-0 win over Aston Villa and a 2-2 draw with the unbeaten champions Preston before 10,000 at Turf Moor kept Burnley clear of the bottom. Gallocher left for Accrington in March. In the same month Jack Yates became Burnley's first England player, scoring a hat-trick against Ireland.

chatham-town.hook: Kent amateurs who knocked Nottingham Forest out on an open army field and reached the 1889 quarter-finals.
history: Chatham are a young Kent club with army roots, wearing red and blue hoops. In 1888-89 they came through four qualifying rounds, then beat South Shore and, after three games, Nottingham Forest to reach the last eight, the best run of any southern amateur side that year. Their home was an open military field where no admission could be taken, so visiting clubs travelled for nothing; the complaints led the FA to require enclosed grounds, and Chatham moved to Maidstone Road in 1889.

crewe-alexandra.hook: The railway-works club, FA Cup semi-finalists in 1888 and founders of the rival Combination.
history: Crewe Alexandra grew from the cricket club of the railway works and play beside the station. They reached the FA Cup semi-final in 1888, helped by a protest about a low crossbar that overturned a defeat by Swifts. Their secretary J. G. Hall led the clubs left out of the League into the Combination, and Crewe's own ground was picked for the 1889 Cup semi-final. On the pitch, 1888-89 brought a heavy Cup replay defeat by Halliwell.

derby-county.hook: A football club started to pay the cricket club's bills, playing in amber, chocolate and blue on a racecourse.
history: Derby County was born in 1884 in the offices of Derbyshire County Cricket Club, which had just lost every Championship match and needed winter income. Committee man William Morley proposed a football section, the county FA turned down "Derbyshire County" as too long, and the new club took the cricket club's amber, chocolate and blue and its ground at the Racecourse.

The start was rough: a 6-0 friendly defeat at Great Lever and a 7-0 home loss to Walsall Town in the club's first FA Cup tie. But a cup win over Aston Villa in 1885-86 made Derby's name, and helped earn them a seat among the League's twelve founders in 1888.
The early sides were full of local men and cricketers, from Derbyshire captain William Chatterton to future Wisden cricketer Levi Wright, with Scottish centre-forward Alex Higgins leading the line.

seasons.1888-89: Derby opened the League on 8 September 1888 at Bolton, came back from 3-0 down and won 6-3; George Bakewell scored the club's first League goal and 17-year-old Harry Plackett was the youngest player in the League. Then came a club-record eight straight defeats between September and December, including 5-0 losses at West Bromwich and Preston and 6-2 at Everton and Accrington. The spring was better: Higgins scored four in a 5-2 win over Aston Villa on 9 March, and Derby won 5-3 at Notts County a week later. Lol Plackett was the only ever-present and Higgins top-scored with 11 League goals. Derby finished 10th.

derby-junction.hook: School old boys from Derby who beat the Cup holders Blackburn Rovers in 1888 and reached the semi-finals.
history: Derby Junction began as the old boys of Junction Street School and stayed firmly amateur. In 1887-88 they shocked the Cup holders Blackburn Rovers 2-1 on a frozen, bumpy pitch to reach the FA Cup semi-final, lost to West Bromwich Albion, and then became the first Derby side to win the Derbyshire Senior Cup. In 1888-89 they struggled in the Combination and lost a Derby derby to the League's County in the Cup.

everton.hook: A Methodist chapel side turned big-city club, with the League's biggest crowds at Anfield and a landlord it would soon fall out with.
history: Everton began in 1878 as St Domingo's, the football side of a Methodist chapel in the Everton district of Liverpool, and in November 1879 the members met at the Queen's Head and renamed the club after their neighbourhood. They played first on an open pitch in Stanley Park, then at Priory Road, until the crowds grew too big and too noisy for the landlord.

In 1884 they moved to a field at Anfield, soon bought by the brewer and Tory alderman John Houlding. Stands went up, gates swelled, and Everton became one of the best-supported clubs in England. Money brought professionals, some of them from Scotland, and trouble: in 1887-88 the FA threw Everton out of the Cup and suspended them for a month for fielding ineligible players.

Everton were founder members of the Football League in 1888. They spent heavily on new men such as Nick Ross from Preston and young Edgar Chadwick from Blackburn, and used 35 players in the first season, still a club record. Within three seasons they were champions, and within four they had left Anfield after a rent dispute with Houlding, who founded Liverpool to fill it.

seasons.1888-89: Everton won their first two games at Anfield, George Fleming scoring both goals in the 2-1 win over Accrington on opening day, but were beaten 6-2 at Bolton. October brought the best spell, a 2-0 home win over Aston Villa and two wins over Derby (4-2 away, then 6-2 at home with an Alex McKinnon hat-trick). The defence was weakened when right-back Alec Dick was suspended for striking an opponent at Notts County in November. After a 3-2 win over Burnley in late November Everton won only twice more; 15,000 saw Preston win 2-0 at Anfield in January. They finished eighth, one place clear of re-election. Chadwick, ever-present, was top league scorer with six.

grimsby-town.hook: Lincolnshire's leading club, in chocolate and blue, in its last season at Clee Park.
history: Grimsby Town began as Grimsby Pelham in 1878, named after the Earl of Yarborough's family, and soon became the strongest club in Lincolnshire. In 1888-89 they played in the short-lived Combination and battled through four qualifying rounds, including three games with Lincoln City. They beat Sunderland Albion and then hosted Preston, the unbeaten champions, before leaving Clee Park for Abbey Park.

halliwell.hook: Bolton's other professional club, factory-backed, full of Scots, and left outside the League.
history: Halliwell, from the north-west of Bolton, went professional early with the help of local mill owners and by 1885 had more Scottish players than almost anyone in England. They won the Bolton Charity Cup in 1887, but the League wanted only one Bolton club and chose the Wanderers. In 1888-89 they played in the Combination, thrashed Crewe in a Cup replay, and beat weakened Bolton and Burnley sides in the Lancashire Cup before losing to Birmingham St George's.

heeley.hook: The Wednesday's first great rivals, still amateur, who won four qualifying rounds in 1888-89.
history: Heeley, a church club from the Sheffield suburb of the same name, was one of the leading sides of the Sheffield Rules era and played The Wednesday in the first Sheffield Challenge Cup final in 1877. Jack Hunter, later of Blackburn Olympic, won England caps here. By 1888 the professionals had passed the amateurs by, but Heeley still won four qualifying ties before losing at Walsall.

linfield.hook: Belfast mill workers' club that beat Bolton, played a Christmas Day cup tie, and drew at Nottingham Forest.
history: Linfield Athletic were formed in 1886 by workers at the Linfield Mill in Sandy Row and quickly gained a name for a passing game new to Irish football. In 1888-89 they knocked out a Football League side, Bolton Wanderers, in qualifying, beat Cliftonville on Christmas Day, and drew 2-2 at Nottingham Forest. Then they had to concede the tie over an ineligible player; the clubs kept it quiet and played the Belfast "replay" as a friendly, which Linfield won before a large, unaware crowd.

long-eaton-rangers.hook: A small Derbyshire town club that won the 1887 Birmingham Senior Cup against West Bromwich Albion.
history: Long Eaton Rangers formed in 1881 and were unbeaten at home for two seasons. Their high point came in 1887, when a late deflected free kick beat West Bromwich Albion in the Birmingham Senior Cup final at Wellington Road. The League judged the town too small, so the Rangers joined the Combination in 1888-89 and did well there. The FA Cup draw was unkind as usual, sending them to Birmingham St George's.

nottingham-forest.hook: The Garibaldi reds of 1865, turned down by the League and knocked out of the Cup by Chatham on a neutral ground.
history: Forest were founded in 1865 by shinty players at the Clinton Arms and chose "Garibaldi red" after the Italian patriot's redshirts, the first club to wear red officially. They gave Arsenal a set of red shirts in 1886, and their best player, the England centre forward Tinsley Lindley, came home from Cambridge in 1888. The League refused to admit them, so 1888-89 is a season of friendlies and Cup ties, ending with an upset loss to Chatham after three games.

notts-county.hook: The oldest club in the League: gentlemen amateurs and county cricketers learning to live with professionals.
history: Notts County date their birth to 1862, when a group of Nottingham gentlemen began meeting to kick a ball about in The Park; they organised properly in December 1864. That makes Notts the oldest club in the Football League, and their meetings with Nottingham Forest, first played in 1866, one of the oldest fixtures in the game.

Notts were an amateur club for twenty years, and among the strongest. Harry Cursham's FA Cup goals for the club are still a competition record, and Harwood Greenhalgh was the club's first England player in 1872. In 1885, when the FA legalised professionalism, Notts registered six professionals straight away.

In 1888 the club, then playing in chocolate and blue at the Trent Bridge cricket ground, joined the new Football League. Its sides mixed Nottinghamshire cricketers like William Gunn and Mordecai Sherwin with professionals from Scotland and the local works teams.

seasons.1888-89: A difficult first League season. Albert Moore scored the club's first League goal in a 2-1 defeat at Everton, but Notts lost 9-1 at Aston Villa and 7-0 at home to Preston, and conceded 73 goals, the worst record in the League. The bright spot was 27 October, when Bob Jardine became the first man to score five in a League match in a 6-1 win over Burnley. Harry Daft and Jardine shared top scoring with nine each, and Alf Shelton missed only one League game. The cup brought more joy: four qualifying wins and a 2-0 defeat of Old Brightonians before a 3-2 loss at The Wednesday. Sherwin, the 17-stone cricketer-goalkeeper, played his last game in December and Cursham announced his retirement in January. Notts finished 11th, ahead of Stoke only on goal average.

notts-rangers.hook: Nottingham's third club: Notts Cup holders, Combination pace-setters, and gone by 1890.
history: Notts Rangers grew from a church side, St James, into a club good enough to win the Nottinghamshire Senior Cup in 1888 and 1889. The FA made them one of the clubs exempt from qualifying in 1888-89, to some surprise, and they took The Wednesday to a replay. In the Combination they had the best record of any club that played its full programme, yet crowds were tiny next to Notts County and Forest, and their best players drifted away.

old-brightonians.hook: Brighton College old boys from London who fought through four qualifying rounds to meet a League club.
history: The Old Brightonians are former pupils of Brighton College playing out of London. Their best FA Cup run took them to the third round in 1887-88, and in 1888-89, the first season of qualifying rounds, they won four ties to reach the first round proper, one of only two old-boy sides to do so. They went down 2-0 at Notts County, the first goal an own goal and the second at the death.

old-carthusians.hook: Charterhouse old boys, 1881 FA Cup winners, and home of England's "Morning and Afternoon" full-backs.
history: The Old Carthusians gather the old boys of Charterhouse, one of the schools that shaped the passing game. They won the FA Cup in 1881, but their 1883 semi-final loss to the working men of Blackburn Olympic marked the end of the old boys' era. Their side still holds England internationals, among them the Walters brothers and William Cobbold, and in 1888-89 they pushed the League's Wolves all the way before losing 4-3.

old-westminsters.hook: Westminster School old boys, often London's best cup side, who ran a League club to 4-3 in a snowstorm.
history: The Old Westminsters gather the former pupils of Westminster School, whose cloister football helped shape the passing game. Formed as a proper club in 1880, they reached three FA Cup quarter-finals in the 1880s and were usually the strongest side in the capital, but by 1888 the professionals of the north and Midlands had left the old boys behind. They remain a force in the London cups and won the London Charity Cup in 1888-89.

preston-north-end.hook: The Invincibles: a Scottish-built passing machine that won the first League unbeaten and the Cup without conceding.
history: North End started out as a Preston cricket club in 1863. In 1875 it leased a field at Deepdale Farm, and it is still there today. Rugby was tried and dropped. Association football was first played in 1878, and in 1880 the members voted to make it the club's main winter game.

The club grew under William Sudell, a mill manager and the club's chairman. In the early 1880s he brought skilled Scots to Preston and found them jobs at his mill. In 1884 Upton Park complained that Preston were paying players, and North End withdrew from the FA Cup. Sudell then pushed hard for professionalism, and the FA legalised it in 1885.

By 1888 Preston were the team to beat. They had won an FA Cup tie 26-0 against Hyde in 1887 and reached the 1888 Cup Final. In the League's first season they did not lose a match, and they won the Cup without conceding a goal. That made them the first side to win the "Double".

seasons.1888-89: North End opened with a 5-2 home win over Burnley on 8 September. Dewhurst and Gordon scored on their League debuts. Two 7-0 wins followed: at home to Stoke (6 Oct) and at Notts County (3 Nov), where Gordon scored a hat-trick. Only four teams took a point off them: Accrington (0-0), Aston Villa (1-1), and Burnley and Blackburn (both 2-2). John Goodall led the scoring with 21 league goals (his own article says 20) and Jimmy Ross scored 19. James Trainer kept goal in the League. For the Cup, the amateur doctor Robert Mills-Roberts played instead, and Preston went five ties without conceding. In the semi-final David Russell's goal beat West Brom. In the Final at the Oval, Fred Dewhurst (15'), Ross (25') and Sam Thomson (70') beat Wolves 3-0. Dewhurst captained the side that day.

sheffield-wednesday.hook: Sheffield's leading club, newly professional and in a ground of its own, reaching the Cup quarter-finals without a league.
history: The Wednesday grew out of a cricket club in 1867 and soon dominated Sheffield football, winning the first Sheffield Challenge Cup. In 1887 their best players threatened to walk out and form a professional Sheffield Rovers; the club gave in, turned professional, and built Olive Grove so it no longer had to share gates with Bramall Lane. Without a league in 1888-89, Wednesday made the FA Cup quarter-finals, beating Notts County along the way.

small-heath.hook: Birmingham's "Heathens", the first football club to become a limited company, in 1888.
history: Small Heath Alliance started in 1875 on waste ground in Bordesley Green and settled at a rented field off the Coventry Road in 1877. They turned professional in 1885, reached the FA Cup semi-final in 1886, and in 1888 became the first football club to form a limited company with a board, dropping "Alliance" from the name. In 1888-89 they won three qualifying ties at home, scoring 16 goals, before losing narrowly to the Cup holders West Bromwich Albion.

south-shore.hook: Blackpool's senior club, 1886 Cup giant-killers, whose trip to Chatham changed the FA Cup rules.
history: South Shore are the senior club of Blackpool, paying players half-a-crown a match since 1885-86. That season they beat Notts County at home and reached the FA Cup quarter-finals. In 1888-89 they played in the short-lived Combination, then travelled to Chatham for the Cup, where the open field let the hosts charge no admission and the visitors got no share of a gate; their complaint led the FA to require enclosed grounds. Their 1889 bid for the Football League got no votes, and a new local club, Blackpool, began to overtake them.

stoke.hook: The Potteries club whose secretary-manager ran the whole Football League, and which finished bottom of it twice.
history: Stoke trace their roots to railway apprentices who had learned the game at Charterhouse School; the club calls 1863 its birth year, though the first match on record is from 1868. In 1878 they merged with the Stoke Victoria Athletic Club and moved to the Victoria Ground, which would be home for more than a century.

Stoke won the first two Staffordshire Cups (1877, 1878), turned professional in August 1885 and won their first FA Cup tie, 10-0 against Caernarfon Wanderers, in 1886-87. Players started on half a crown a week and won a rise to five shillings by threatening to strike.

When the Football League was formed in 1888, Stoke's secretary-manager Harry Lockett went to the London meeting and came back as the League's first secretary. On the pitch, the club found the new competition hard going.

seasons.1888-89: Stoke opened the League with a 2-0 home defeat by West Bromwich Albion before 4,524, and Frank Staton scored the club's first League goal in a 5-1 loss at Aston Villa. The first win, 3-0 over Notts County, came in week three with two goals from Billy Tunnicliffe. On 6 October the first team lost 7-0 at Preston with two borrowed Preston reserves after two men missed the train, while the reserves lost an FA Cup tie to non-League Warwick County on the same day. A 4-3 win over Burnley, a 3-0 double over Notts County and a 2-1 win over Blackburn were the high points. Captain Tommy Clare, Alf Underwood and goalkeeper Bill Rowley held the defence together, and Scottish forward Bob McSkimming played every game and top-scored with six. Stoke finished bottom on goal average.

sunderland-albion.hook: A breakaway formed in March 1888 by Sunderland's own founder, James Allan, and Sunderland AFC's bitter rival.
history: Sunderland Albion were born out of a row: when Sunderland AFC were thrown out of the 1887-88 Cup for fielding Scots under false names, the club's founder James Allan left and set up a rival, officially amateur, with jobs in local pubs and glassworks for its players. Twice in 1888-89 the cup draws paired the two Sunderland clubs, and twice Sunderland AFC withdrew. Albion won the Durham Challenge Cup in their first season, though they lost at Grimsby in the FA Cup.

swifts.hook: Slough's gentlemen amateurs, three-time FA Cup semi-finalists and home of the Bambridge brothers.
history: The Swifts are a club of Berkshire and Buckinghamshire gentlemen who reached FA Cup semi-finals in 1874, 1876 and 1886. Charles Bambridge, the most capped of the three Bambridge brothers, made them famous, and the Scottish star Andrew Watson also turned out for them. They play at the Dolphin Ground in Slough and still beat good sides, but amateur football is shrinking around them.

walsall.hook: A brand-new merger of two old Walsall rivals, in its first season at the Chuckery.
history: Walsall Town Swifts were formed in early 1888 when the town's two senior clubs, Walsall Town and Walsall Swifts, joined forces at the Chuckery. Their first game was the Birmingham Charity Cup final against Aston Villa, and that summer they beat Burnley and held West Bromwich Albion in front of 7,000. In 1888-89 they finished third in the Midland Association and won an FA Cup tie before a heavy defeat at Wolves.

west-bromwich-albion.hook: The FA Cup holders: a works team of local lads, led by the teenage winger Billy Bassett.
history: West Bromwich Albion grew out of a works team: in 1878 young men from Salter's spring factory began playing as the West Bromwich Strollers, and two years later took the name Albion from a district of the town. They tried a rainbow of colours before settling on blue-and-white stripes in 1885, the year they turned professional and moved to Stoney Lane.

Albion became the cup-fighters of the Midlands. They lost the FA Cup final in 1886 and 1887, then in March 1888 beat the great Preston North End 2-1 at the Kennington Oval, Jem Bayliss and George Woodhall scoring and 19-year-old Billy Bassett running the show. Almost the whole side was local, and its professionals earned about ten shillings a week.
As Cup holders they entered the first Football League season with most of that team intact: "Long Bob" Roberts in goal, the Perry and Horton brothers, Timmins, Pearson and Bassett.

seasons.1888-89: Albion began with a 2-0 win at Stoke, Joe Wilson scoring the club's first league goal late on, and a 5-0 home win over Derby (Pearson three) in early October. Defeats to Preston, home and away (0-3, 0-5 on Boxing Day), and a 1-5 home loss to Bolton showed the gap to the leaders, but Bassett and Pearson, 11 league goals each, kept them mid-table and they finished sixth. The FA Cup was again the highlight: Walter Perry's hat-trick beat Burnley 5-1, and Albion won 10-1 at Chatham before 17,000, but the semi-final was lost 0-1 to Preston at Bramall Lane in front of 22,688. Roberts, Pearson and Timmins played every league game.

witton.hook: Blackburn's third club, a professional side with no league after it walked out of the Combination.
history: Witton began as St Mark's, a cricket club's football side near Blackburn, and grew into a professional outfit that reached the Lancashire Cup semi-finals. Shut out of the Football League because Blackburn already had Rovers, the club joined the rival Combination and then quit it as second-rate. That left Witton playing friendlies, mostly away, in 1888-89, and suffering heavy defeats to Everton, Darwen and Preston, though they ran Aston Villa close in the Cup.

wolverhampton-wanderers.hook: A church-school team grown up: local lads, schoolmaster captains and a run to the first League-era Cup Final.
history: Wolves started out in 1877 as a schoolboys' team at St Luke's in Blakenhall, playing with a ball their headmaster had given them. Two years later they joined up with the local Wanderers cricket club and took the town's name. In 1881 they moved to Dudley Road, across from the Fighting Cocks Inn.

The club stayed local. Its founders, Baynton and Brodie, were still in the side in 1888, and secretary Jack Addenbrooke had taught at St Luke's. In 1884 Wolves won the Wrekin Cup, their first trophy. By 1888 they were strong enough to be one of the twelve founders of the Football League, and they finished third in its first season.

seasons.1888-89: Wolves were at home to Aston Villa on 8 September, one of the League's opening fixtures, and drew 1-1. Their goal was an own goal by Villa's Gershom Cox. In their next home game Preston beat them 4-0, but over the season they were one of the most consistent sides, with a 5-0 win over Everton and doubles over West Brom and Stoke. Harry Wood was top scorer with 13 league goals, and Dickie Baugh and Harry Allen played every league match. The Cup run was the high point: five ties, a record 10,000 crowd at Dudley Road for The Wednesday, and a semi-final win over the old Cup kings Blackburn after a replay at Crewe. In the Final at the Oval, with Brodie as captain, they lost 3-0 to the Invincibles.

wrexham.hook: The oldest club in Wales, first Welsh Cup winners, back under their own name after a forced re-formation.
history: Formed by cricketers at the Turf Tavern in 1864, Wrexham are the oldest club in Wales and play at the Racecourse, where Wales staged its first home international. They won the first Welsh Cup in 1878, but crowd trouble at an 1883 FA Cup tie got the club expelled and it had to start again as Wrexham Olympic. In 1888-89 they won four qualifying rounds to reach the first round proper for the first time.

john-goodall-1863.bio: Centre-forward born in London to Scottish parents, raised in Kilmarnock; at Preston since 1885, England cap 1888 (14 caps, 12 goals by 1898). Top scorer of the first League season (21 League goals per the season page, 20 per his article). Left for Derby in 1889.

fred-dewhurst-1863.bio: Amateur inside forward from Fulwood, a schoolmaster at Preston Catholic College; 9 England caps, 11 goals (1886-89). 12 League goals; captain in the 1889 Final and scorer of its first goal. Died 1895, aged 31.

jimmy-ross-1866.bio: Edinburgh inside forward, Nick Ross's younger brother, scorer of 7 in the 26-0 over Hyde (1887). 19 League goals and a goal in the Final; champion again in 1890.

james-trainer-1863.bio: Wrexham-born goalkeeper, 20 Wales caps (1887-99); kept goal in 20 League games and won four titles with Preston. ("Prince of Goalkeepers" is often attached to him but was not found in a source; not used.)

robert-mills-roberts-1862.bio: Welsh amateur goalkeeper and surgeon, 8 Wales caps; kept goal in all five Cup ties without conceding.

bob-howarth-1865.bio: Preston-born full-back and solicitor, 4 England caps (1886-94); 18 League and 5 Cup apps. To Everton 1891.

robert-holmes-1867.bio: Preston-born left-back, ever-present (22); 7 England caps 1888-95, at the club until 1902 (300 League games).

jack-gordon-1861.bio: Winger from Bridge of Weir, at Preston from 1884; 10 League goals incl. a hat-trick in the 7-0 at Notts County and a goal on day one.

johnny-graham-1857.bio: Wing-half from Coylton, Scotland cap 1884; ever-present in the Double season.

david-russel-1863.bio: Tough-tackling centre-half from Beith (18 apps); scored the semi-final winner v WBA. To Forest 1890.

sam-thomson-1862.bio: Winger from Lugar, 2 Scotland caps (1884); scored Preston's third in the Final.

george-drummond-1865.bio: Edinburgh utility man and left winger, at Preston 1883-99 (12 League apps plus 4 in the Cup).

sandy-robertson-1860.bio: Edinburgh half-back, 21 of 22 League games (3 goals); to Royal Arsenal 1890.

archie-goodall-1865.bio: John's Belfast-born brother: 2 apps, 1 goal, then to Villa on 1 Oct 1888 (first in-season League transfer).

archie-hunter-1859.bio: Ayrshire forward at Villa since 1878, captain of the 1887 Cup winners and a scorer in every round; his 36 FA Cup goals are still a club record. Never capped (Scotland did not pick England-based men). Collapsed during a match in 1890, died 1894; a Football League 100 Legend.

dennis-hodgetts-1863.bio: Birmingham winger who scored the first goal of the 1887 Final; 6 England caps (1888-94), 10 goals in 1888-89; League champion 1894 and 1896, Cup winner 1895.

albert-allen-1867.bio: Aston-born inside forward, hat-trick on his only England cap (1888); top scorer (19) incl. the club's first League hat-trick (9-1 v Notts County). Died 1899.

jimmy-warner-1865.bio: Lozells-born goalkeeper, 1887 Cup winner (21 League apps).

albert-brown-1862.bio: Right winger and 1887 Cup winner, ever-present in 1888-89 (7 League goals); at Villa 1884-94.

tommy-green-1863.bio: Worcester-born forward, ex-WBA; scored Villa's first League goal and played all 22 games (15 goals).

gershom-cox-1863.bio: Birmingham full-back, ever-present; his own goal at Wolves on 8 Sep 1888 was long listed as the League's first goal.

harry-devey-1864.bio: Birmingham centre-half who missed one game.

harry-yates-1861.bio: Walsall-born defensive wing-half, 1887 Cup winner (13 apps).

john-brodie-1862.bio: Co-founded St Luke's at 15, a schoolteacher; captain in the 1889 Final and England captain on his 1889 debut (3 caps). 11 League goals.

harry-allen-1866.bio: Walsall-born centre-half, 5 England caps 1888-90, ever-present; later captain and scorer of the 1893 Final winner. Died 1895.

dickie-baugh-1864.bio: Right-back from Staveley, 2 England caps, ever-present; three Finals (winner 1893, captain 1896).

charlie-mason-1863.bio: Wolverhampton-born full-back and founder member, nearly 300 games, 3 England caps (1887-90).

jack-baynton-1859.bio: Founder-era player and early secretary, Wrekin Cup captain 1884, now goalkeeper (18 apps, played in the Final). Left April 1889.

harry-wood-1868.bio: Walsall-born inside forward, top scorer (13); 3 England caps (1890-96), 1893 Cup winner.

arthur-lowder-1863.bio: Local left-half from St Luke's (1882); England cap Feb 1889.

albert-fletcher-1867.bio: Right-half, 2 England caps (1889, 1890); later Wolves trainer until 1920.

tommy-hunter-1863.bio: Walsall-born winger (20 apps, 4 goals), played in the Final.

david-wykes-1867.bio: Joined Aug 1888 (4 League + 3 Cup goals); 1893 Cup winner, died 1895.

tommy-knight-1865.bio: Local inside-right, 7 League and 5 Cup goals.

jimmy-forrest-1864.bio: Blackburn-born half-back, the first professional to play for England (11 caps 1884-90) and a five-time FA Cup winner (1884-86, 1890, 1891); later a director.

herby-arthur-1863.bio: Blackburn-born goalkeeper, 7 England caps (1885-87), four FA Cups; remembered as the man left alone on the pitch at Burnley in 1891.

fergus-suter-1857.bio: Glasgow stonemason often called the first professional footballer; four Finals, three wins. One League game in 1888-89 (22 Dec).

john-forbes-1862.bio: Vale of Leven full-back, 5 Scotland caps; Cup winner 1890 and 1891.

jack-southworth-1866.bio: Blackburn centre-forward and professional violinist; top scorer (17 League + 4 Cup), four v Villa. 3 England caps, a goal in each; later the first to 100 League goals.

william-townley-1866.bio: Blackburn-born left winger (8 League goals); 2 England caps, first Cup Final hat-trick (1890); later a coach in Germany.

nat-walton-1867.bio: Preston-born inside forward, 1886 Cup winner (10 League goals); England cap 1890.

jimmy-douglas-1859.bio: Renfrew half-back, Scotland cap 1880, at Rovers since 1880.

harry-fecitt-1864.bio: Blackburn forward, 1885/86 Cup winner, back from Accrington (12 League goals).

joe-beverley-1856.bio: Blackburn full-back, ex-Olympic, 3 England caps (1884); briefly the League's oldest player.

robert-haresnape-1866.bio: Winger, Cup hero of the season (hat-trick in the 8-1 v Villa). To Burnley 1889.

kenny-davenport-1862.bio: Bolton-born inside right at the club since 1883, England caps 1885 and 1890; ever-present (11 goals). Since 2013 credited with the first Football League goal (8 Sep 1888, 3:47 pm, Pikes Lane; plaque 2016).

bob-roberts-1864.bio: Welsh wing-half from Penycae, at Bolton since 1884-85, 9 Wales caps; ever-present.

alexander-barbour-1862.bio: Dumbarton striker, 1885 Scottish Cup winner with Renton, 1 Scotland cap; 9 goals in 14.

james-brogan-1864.bio: Scottish forward from Beith, new in 1888; ever-present and top scorer (13).

david-weir-1863.bio: Aldershot-born centre-half/forward from Halliwell (1888); ever-present, 10 goals incl. a hat-trick v Accrington; 2 England caps 1889.

di-jones-1867.bio: Welsh left-back from Chirk (two Welsh Cups); ten years and 228 games at Bolton, captain in the 1894 Final, 14 Wales caps.

john-milne-1866.bio: Ever-present forward/centre-half (6 goals); little else is known.

charlie-harrison-1861.bio: Goalkeeper from Newton Heath (19 apps); went back there in 1889.

harry-tyrer-1868.bio: Winger from Halsall, both goals in the 6-2 over Everton.

billy-bassett-1869.bio: Local outside right, 19, the star of the 1888 Cup final and an England international from 1888 (16 caps, 8 goals to 1896); joint top scorer (11). Cup winner again 1892, later chairman; a Football League 100 Legend.

bob-roberts-1859.bio: Local goalkeeper, 6 ft 4 in, the club's first international (England 1887, 1888, 1890), 1888 Cup winner; ever-present.

jem-bayliss-1865.bio: Tipton wing-half/forward who captained the 1888 Cup winners and opened the scoring in the Final; England cap 1891.

george-woodhall-1864.bio: Local forward who scored the 1888 Final winner; 2 England caps (1888).

tom-pearson-1866.bio: Local inside left, in the 1887, 1888 and 1892 Finals; ever-present and joint top scorer (11). 72 goals in 138 games.

charlie-perry-1864.bio: Local centre-half; Cup winner 1888 and 1892, 3 England caps, captain from 1891, later a director.

george-timmins-1863.bio: Left-half at the club from 1880, three Finals; ever-present; called "a hard, fearless man".

joe-wilson-1865.bio: Handsworth outside left, 1888 Cup winner, scorer of the club's first League goal (at Stoke); later a League referee and a goldsmith.

walter-perry-1865.bio: Local inside forward, 4 League goals and 6 in the Cup (hat-trick v Burnley).

billy-hendry-1865.bio: Scottish centre-forward, 19 (16 apps); to Stoke April 1889.

george-haworth-1863.bio: Accrington-born half-back at the club 1882-92, 5 England caps (1887-90), 1885 FA Cup winner on loan to Blackburn; captain in 1889-90.

joe-lofthouse-1864.bio: Blackburn-born winger, four FA Cups with Blackburn and 7 England caps (1885-87); one season here (21 apps). Nationally a tier-4 name, at this club a newcomer.

johnny-horne-1862.bio: Amateur goalkeeper from Huncoat, a chemist; ever-present, held Preston to their only goalless League game of the season.

jim-bonar-1866.bio: Glasgow-born forward at the club since 1884 (17 apps).

john-kirkham-1869.bio: Forward, 19, two on debut in the 5-5 at Blackburn, 12 goals in 19; became the club's record appearance maker and scorer.

billy-barbour-1865.bio: Kilmarnock centre-forward, top scorer (13); his move from Queen of the South was reportedly paid in groceries.

bob-brand-1865.bio: Scottish forward, 11 goals in 16, the club's first League hat-trick (6-2 v Derby).

john-stevenson-1862.bio: Glasgow full-back, ever-present; 81 League apps to 1893.

john-mclellan-1863.bio: Edinburgh full-back from Hearts, at the club 1888-93.

james-tattersall-1864.bio: Accrington-born defender, about 100 League apps to 1893.

nick-ross-1863.bio: Edinburgh-born full-back, Preston's captain and star, lured to Everton for a reported £10 a month; the first full-back to score a League goal. Back to Preston in 1889; called a "footballing genius" by William Pickford (1906); died of TB in 1894. At Preston his tier would be 5.

george-dobson-1862.bio: Bolton-born right-back, one of Everton's first professionals (about 130 pre-League games); injury ended his career in 1889. In the Gwladys Street Hall of Fame.

george-farmer-1865.bio: Oswestry-born wing-half with 2 Wales caps, at the club since 1885 (81 pre-League goals).

robert-smalley-1865.bio: Darwen goalkeeper, first choice since Oct 1887.

alec-dick-1865.bio: Kilmarnock full-back, the first Scottish professional Everton signed; suspended after striking an opponent at Notts County, Nov 1888.

john-weir-1865.bio: Crossmyloof half-back, suspended in 1887 over professionalism, then reinstated (16 apps).

johnny-holt-1865.bio: 5 ft 5 in centre-half from Church, signed from Bootle 1888; Everton's first England cap (1890, 10 in all), 1891 champion, Gwladys Street Hall of Fame; known for crafty fouls.

edgar-chadwick-1869.bio: Inside left, 19, from Blackburn (1 Jul 1888); ever-present and top scorer (6). 270 games, 97 goals, 1891 champion, 7 England caps; later coached the Netherlands.

alf-milward-1865.bio: Outside left from Great Marlow, 18, debut Nov 1888; later 201 games, 84 goals, 1891 champion, 4 England caps.

dan-friel-1860.bio: Scottish centre-half from Bonhill, captain since 1883 with 300+ games for the club. The only ever-present of 1888-89 (22); left late 1889.

sandy-lang-1865.bio: Scottish full-back from Bridge of Weir, captain when League football came to Turf Moor (21 apps). First Burnley man to 100 games (1893), scorer of the club's first League penalty (1891); stayed to 1895.

john-yates-1861.bio: Blackburn-born left winger, an 1883 FA Cup winner with Blackburn Olympic. 21 apps, 5 goals; Burnley's first England player, hat-trick on his only cap (v Ireland, 2 Mar 1889).

pat-gallocher-1865.bio: Quick, tricky Scottish inside forward from Johnstone; scored Burnley's first League goal and was the club's top scorer in all competitions (9). Left for Accrington in March 1889.

jack-keenan-1865.bio: Strong half-back from Clitheroe, a local man in a mostly Scottish side (20 apps); at Burnley 1884-93 and close to an England cap.

william-bury-1865.bio: Hard-tackling full-back from Darwen, Lang's partner (20 apps).

bill-mcfettridge-1865.bio: Robust Govan half-back who played a Scottish Cup final at 16 (1880); 16 apps, at Burnley 1886-93.

jack-abrahams-1865.bio: Barrhead wing-half at the club since 1885 (13 apps); scored the winner v Notts County, 29 Dec 1888.

fred-poland-1865.bio: Dundee centre forward, scorer of the club's second League goal (9 apps, 5 goals). Single source: kept goal in the 1-7 at Blackburn.

william-tait-1864.bio: Glasgow inside forward who scored the first Football League hat-trick (15 Sep 1888, at Bolton; one fan source says two goals). Suspended for drinking after it and gone by late October.

alec-brady-1865.bio: Scottish inside forward from Cathcart, credited with 7 League goals (some apps may be William Brady's). Later League champion with Everton (1891), Scottish Cup with Celtic (1892), FA Cup with Wednesday (1896).

william-mckay-1865.bio: Scottish inside forward from Hearts (Nov 1888); 7 goals in 14 apps, the team's best League tally.

walter-cox-1865.bio: Scottish goalkeeper from Leith Harp (Nov 1888): 13 League games and both cup ties.

william-brady-1870.bio: Forward, scored in the cup v Old Westminsters; records tangled with Alec Brady's.

robert-kay-1865.bio: Goalkeeper at the club since 1884; 5 apps, dropped after heavy defeats.

william-smith-1865.bio: Goalkeeper from Haggate, 3 apps including the opening day.

ross-mcmahon-1865.bio: Scottish centre forward; 2 League apps (injured in both) and both cup ties.

thomas-midgley-1860.bio: Captain of Burnley Rovers at the 1882 switch from rugby; 1 app (at Stoke) aged about 32.

alex-higgins-1863.bio: Kilmarnock centre-forward and former miner, Scotland cap in 1885 (hat-trick on debut). Top scorer with 11 League goals in 21 apps, including Derby's first four-goal game (v Villa).

george-bakewell-1865.bio: Derby-born winger, thin and fast, the club's second-ever signing; scored Derby's first League goal (16 apps, 6 goals).

benjamin-spilsbury-1865.bio: Repton and Cambridge amateur, 3 England caps (5 goals), scorer of the club's first recorded goal (1884). One League game (1 goal) and the cup tie in 1888-89.

william-chatterton-1861.bio: Derbyshire cricket captain, later an England Test player; in the club's first FA Cup tie (1884). 5 apps, 1 goal.

lawrence-plackett-1869.bio: Forward from Breaston, the only ever-present (22 apps, 7 goals); two on the opening day. Released 1889.

lewis-cooper-1864.bio: Belper forward, 8 goals in 15 apps; 23 goals in 50 apps over 1888-91.

walter-roulstone-1864.bio: Left half from Castle Donington (21 apps); first Derby player to 100 League games (118 by 1894).

arthur-latham-1863.bio: Coventry-born full-back, an automatic choice (20 apps); at Derby 1886-1901.

albert-williamson-1864.bio: Right half from Sawley, a regular (19 apps).

haydn-morley-1864.bio: Derby-born left-back, cricketer and club pioneer; Notts County then Derby (4 apps, 2 cup ties). Captained The Wednesday in the 1890 Cup final.

levi-wright-1864.bio: Oxford-born teacher and Derbyshire batsman, later a Wisden Cricketer of the Year; 4 apps, 1 goal.

archibald-ferguson-1863.bio: Edinburgh full-back from Hearts, a long kicker (16 apps); later emigrated to the USA.

joseph-marshall-1863.bio: Goalkeeper from Ripley, also a Derbyshire cricketer (16 apps).

harry-plackett-1866.bio: Lol's brother, 17 years 147 days on the opening day: the youngest player in the League (16 apps, 2 goals).

henry-cursham-1863.bio: Amateur forward with 8 England caps (1880-84) and the all-time FA Cup scoring record (49); a voice for dribbling over combination. 8 League apps plus cup ties, retired January 1889.

mordecai-sherwin-1862.bio: Notts cricket captain and England Test wicket-keeper; a goalkeeper of about 17 stone, called "the idol of the crowd", who once turned a cartwheel during a match. 3 cup ties and 1 League game, last on 8 Dec 1888.

harry-daft-1866.bio: Outside left from Radcliffe-on-Trent, son of Richard Daft and a Notts cricketer; joint top scorer (9). First England cap 2 Mar 1889 (5 in all), 1894 FA Cup winner.

charlie-shelton-1864.bio: Left half, England cap in 1888; 15 League apps, 1 goal.

william-gunn-1865.bio: England Test batsman with 2 football caps (1884), co-founder of Gunn & Moore, known for long one-handed throw-ins; 1 League app, director from 1890.

alf-shelton-1865.bio: Nottingham left half known for stamina and heading, signed August 1888; 21 apps, the club's most that season. 6 England caps 1889-92, two Cup finals (1891, 1894).

albert-moore-1865.bio: Nottingham forward with the club since 1883; scored Notts' first League goal on his birthday. Quit in 1889 when his hosiery employer made him choose.

jack-holland-1861.bio: Bulwell tram conductor, first-choice goalkeeper 1886-88 (9 apps).

bob-jardine-1864.bio: Forward, joint top scorer (9); first man to score five in a League game (v Burnley, 27 Oct 1888). Nationality disputed (Scottish; one source: born Newcastle).

george-brown-1863.bio: Nottingham wing half from Forest; 19 apps, 1 goal.

frank-guttridge-1863.bio: Nottingham full-back and Notts/Sussex cricketer (17 apps).

john-clements-1864.bio: Full-back from East Markham, signed Oct 1888 (12 League apps plus cup).

tom-widdowson-1863.bio: Hucknall goalkeeper from Forest, Dec 1888 (12 apps).

edward-may-1865.bio: Hull-born left winger, ex-Port Vale (11 apps, 3 goals).

harry-jackson-1865.bio: Forward at the club 1884-90 (5 League apps, 3 goals).

tommy-clare-1865.bio: Right-back from Congleton and captain in 1888 (21 apps). 4 England caps (1889-94), Alliance champion 1891, 252 Stoke games; later Port Vale manager.

bill-rowley-1863.bio: Hanley goalkeeper who came from Port Vale after a court fight (1886); 21 apps, England caps 1889 and 1892. Later Stoke's secretary-manager and a noted dealmaker.

bob-mcskimming-1864.bio: Kilmarnock forward and sprinter, called Stoke's first Scottish signing; ever-present and top scorer (6).

george-shutt-1864.bio: Fenton half-back, one of Stoke's first professionals, England cap 1886 (21 apps); later a referee.

jimmy-sayer-1865.bio: Outside right from Mexborough, England cap 1887, named by fans for his pace (7 apps, 1 goal).

alf-underwood-1869.bio: Hanley left-back, 19, ever-present (22); England caps 1891 and 1892, a famous pairing with Clare until a knee infection ended his career (1893).

elijah-smith-1863.bio: Stoke-born half-back at the club since 1883, a clergyman, hence the nickname (21 apps).

bob-ramsay-1863.bio: Liverpool-born full-back/half-back from Port Vale (21 apps).

alf-edge-1865.bio: Quick, versatile inside forward from Stone (20 apps, 3 goals); 12 goals in the 1890-91 Alliance title season.

george-lawton-1864.bio: Local right winger (13 apps), scorer of the winner v Burnley.

bob-milarvie-1864.bio: Glasgow forward from Hibernian, Nov 1888 (15 apps, 5 goals; scored on debut).

jimmy-sloane-1864.bio: Govan centre forward on a spell away from Rangers (11 apps, 2 goals).

billy-tunnicliffe-1865.bio: Hanley left winger, both goals in Stoke's first League win (8 apps, 4 goals).

frank-staton-1865.bio: Scored Stoke's first League goal (4 apps, 2 goals).

bill-smalley-1865.bio: Preston reserve lent for the 0-7 at Deepdale.

tinsley-lindley-1865.bio: Amateur England centre forward (14 goals in 13 internationals), back at Forest in 1888 after Cambridge.

billy-betts-1864.bio: Wednesday centre-half and England international, 143 games over two spells.

albert-mumford-1865.bio: Scored Wednesday's goal in the 1890 FA Cup final.

fred-geary-1868.bio: Fast centre forward; later Everton's star (86 goals in 99 games) and an England hat-trick on debut.

chris-charsley-1864.bio: Amateur goalkeeper and police officer; England cap 1893.

caesar-jenkyns-1866.bio: Rugged defender who joined in 1888; later 8 Wales caps; released in 1895 after going for spectators.

andrew-watson-1856.bio: Three Scotland caps (1881-82), widely regarded as the first black international footballer; probably paid by Bootle from 1887.

john-pearson-1868.bio: One-club Crewe man, their only England cap (1892); later refereed the 1911 Cup final.

james-allan-1857.bio: Founder of both Sunderland AFC and the breakaway Sunderland Albion, and a forward for them.

jack-peden-1863.bio: Linfield outside left from 1886, 24 Ireland caps.

charles-wreford-brown-1866.bio: Centre-half, later England captain; credited with coining the word "soccer".

william-moon-1868.bio: Goalkeeper, first capped 1888, 7 caps and once England captain.

bambridge-charles-1858.bio: Very fast winger, 18 England caps (1879-87), twice captain; near the end of his career.

albert-aldridge-1863.bio: Walsall-born England full-back, 1888 FA Cup winner (with WBA).
